item.title: Tax attorney: Investor interest growing in CNMI incentive programs
item.description: Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented. item.content:encoded:
Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented.

Azarvand said she has discussed CNMI investment opportunities with clients who initially sought information about Puerto Rico's tax incentives but became interested in exploring the commonwealth's programs.

"There is definitely interest in the CNMI," she said, noting that one prospective investor traveled from Florida to visit the islands and evaluate opportunities firsthand.

Among those expressing interest are two firms considering operations in the CNMI. One is involved in private equity with a broad range of investment interests, while the other focuses on service-based businesses that can operate remotely and export services outside the islands, she said.

Azarvand declined to identify the companies, saying discussions remain ongoing.

The firms initially viewed CEDA's QC program as their primary incentive option. The QC program provides qualifying businesses tax benefits in exchange for investments that support economic development in the CNMI.

They are now also evaluating opportunities under the economic incentive act, a recently enacted program aimed at attracting new investment and business relocation through additional tax-related benefits.

"They've kind of been wanting to see how this CEIA incentive program goes and see the viability for them as well," Azarvand said.

Azarvand said awareness of the CNMI's incentive programs remains limited among tax professionals on the mainland, including attorneys who specialize in Puerto Rico tax incentives.

"Most tax attorneys I speak with don't even know of the CNMI Qualifying Certificate program," she said.

She said that lack of awareness presents an opportunity for the CNMI to market its incentive programs more aggressively as officials seek to diversify the economy and attract new private-sector investment.

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.title: NWS urges vigilance as dry season begins across Guam and CNMI

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade
item.content:encoded:
The National Weather Service is urging residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to remain weather-aware as drought conditions develop across the region and El Niño keeps the potential for late-season tropical activity above normal.

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade winds, according to the National Weather Service in Guam. Fire danger on Guam has risen to the high category as rainfall remains limited and vegetation continues to dry out.

Despite the dry conditions, Marcus Landon Aydlett, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Guam office, said residents should not overlook the threat of tropical cyclones.

"The risk for late-season tropical cyclones remains elevated through the end of the year and into early 2027 compared with other years," Aydlett said, citing the ongoing El Niño pattern.

No tropical cyclone development is expected during the next seven days, but forecasters said El Niño conditions could continue to influence weather across the western Pacific through the remainder of the year.

The weather service said a wetter pattern may develop later next week and continue into December, providing some relief to drought-affected areas across Micronesia. Residents with low or empty water catchments are encouraged to collect rainwater when showers occur.

item.content:encoded:
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.

Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.

The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.

Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

item.content:encoded:
"I thought I wouldn't survive," says Januka Dhital.

Just minutes before that terrible thought, Dhital was busy preparing snacks. She ran a catering service out of her house in Uttargaya, Nepal, and was getting ready for an event later that day. Her work was interrupted by a man on a scooter, warning of a flood. She stepped outside to look.

"When I turned around, I saw darkness, dust and what looked like the entire hillside coming down," she says.

She grabbed her young son and hopped onto the back of the man's scooter. They raced to higher ground, eventually reaching safety. But she didn't know if her husband and daughter were safe, since they were at work and school when the waters came.

After hours of waiting and searching, they were all reunited. Her husband was naked, covered in blood and badly injured, she says, but alive.

"It felt unbelievable that our family had survived," says Dhital. But the wall of water and mud that descended from the mountains had obliterated their home, along with thousands of others. "We have lost everything. We have nothing now."

Dhital and her family are among the 100,000-some people whose lives have been upended by the devastating floods sparked by glacial melt, a phenomenon made worse by climate change . At least 1,500 have died, and more than 5,000 are still missing. Thousands are still living in temporary shelters or tents.

The flood damaged or destroyed seven health facilities, 23 schools, 10,000 toilets and 64 water systems, according to the United Nations. And there are early signs that malnutrition is spiking as winter approaches.

"The magnitude of devastation is unimaginable," says Shyam Pathak, a chief of health at UNICEF. The din of helicopters circling the wreckage looking for survivors has faded, he says. International attention and aid has fallen too, sources on the ground say, as the response turns to the arduous, but intimate work of helping these communities stitch their lives back together.

This disaster is somewhat unique, Pathak says, in that many of those doing the work are trying to rebuild their own lives at the same time. Dhital is one of them.

In the immediate aftermath of the flood, Dhital and her family moved into a holding center, one of a couple dozen that housed the displaced. They stayed there for about a month before moving into a relative's house. Those days were not easy.

"For almost a month, I felt like I was losing my mind," she says. "More than money, I am in great need of work."

She found that work through Helen Keller Intl , a nonprofit that's helping the response. After a short training program that included mental health support, she began helping her community rebuild. There's a lot to do.

"I go out into the community, we work with postpartum mothers, pregnant women and children under five," says Dhital. "This is the only thing keeping me going right now."

One of her jobs is screening for malnutrition among survivors.

Preliminary data suggest a notable increase. In Naukunda Gaunpalika, for instance, moderate acute malnutrition — a condition that can slow growth, weaken the immune system and become life threatening without treatment — appears to have gone up from 0.8% in June of this year to 8.7% in October, says Pooja Pandey Rana, who directs Hellen Keller's work in Nepal. These are likely conservative estimates too, she says.

"It's a big jump," says Pandey Rana, and likely driven by fallout from the flood.

In addition to losing homes, many families lost the gardens or local farms they relied on for nutritious food. "As a result, they have to depend on dried and packaged foods, such as instant noodles and biscuits," says Dhital. Poor sanitation and lack of clean drinking water is an issue too, she says. And many have lost their livelihoods, so they don't have money to pay for food.

Workers like Dhital are handing out supplies and cash to families in need. In some regions, that's a challenge.

Many of the communities along the flood's path were connected by bridges. More than 100 of them are now destroyed, according to the U.N. And for many living higher up the slopes, mountain roads were a lifeline that have now been severed.

"There still are places, especially in the upper north part of the impacted areas, which have been cut off by the flood," says Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal. "There is still a challenge to deliver food and life saving support to these areas."

Pushmaya Tamang is a community aid worker trying to reach those areas. Often, she must cross the makeshift bridges hastily constructed to make up for the damage.

"The bridge shakes, making it difficult for elderly people to cross," she says. "It becomes dangerous when people try to cross the bridge from both directions at the same time. It almost overturns, making it extremely frightening."

Such damaged infrastructure is a start reminder of what's been lost, she says. Tamang is from a village in Nuwakot that's essentially gone after the floods.

"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction," she says. "The village that was once full of colorful lights and life has now become gloomy and dark."

Tamang's heart is heavy with grief over the loss of her younger sister, too. Many of the families she helps in her work with Helen Keller are also grieving unimaginable loss, she says.

"When we visit other affected families, we do not even know what to say or how to talk to them," she says. "We do not have the words to comfort or console them."

Many survivors need significant mental health support, says Pathak of UNICEF, which is teaming up with other aid organizations to mobilize health workers who can provide counseling. Like Dhital and Tamang, many of them are trying to help rebuild their communities while dealing with their own trauma.

"A hallmark of this response is that the health workers, despite being the victim themselves, are back to the work," says Pathak. "This has helped a lot."

Winter poses distinct challenges for survivors.

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin set to meet in historic summit
item.description: China's President Xi, Russia's President Putin and U.S. President Trump are sitting down for talks in a historic first. Their meeting is happening on the sidelines of a high-powered, regional economic forum in Shenzhen, China. item.content:encoded:
China's President Xi, Russia's President Putin and U.S. President Trump are sitting down for talks in a historic first. Their meeting is happening on the sidelines of a high-powered, regional economic forum in Shenzhen, China. China has described the trilateral meeting of the world leaders as being of, quote, "groundbreaking significance." With us to talk about this moment are NPR correspondent Charles Maynes in Moscow, China correspondent Jennifer Pak and White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram. Jennifer and Deepa are both in Shenzhen. Hi to all three of you.

JENNIFER PAK, BYLINE: Hey. Good morning from here.

PFEIFFER: Deepa, to set the stage here - these are three of the most powerful men in the globe. They control most of the world's nuclear weapons. What is on everyone's agenda?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. Well, that's definitely on the agenda, but for starters, you know, the Iran war remains a top global issue, particularly for Trump. So that's expected to come up in this meeting. But you're right. Trump has been saying for weeks that he wants to discuss denuclearization with Xi and Putin together. Before this trip began, White House officials said that that was going to be the main topic they wanted this meeting to be about, even though they know that China is not really interested in talking about this issue with the U.S. and Russia. A White House official, who was not authorized to speak on the record, said that while they don't expect any agreements to come out of this to reduce the number of nuclear weapons, the administration still thinks it's important for China to engage in this conversation anyway. They said it's, quote, "time for China to step up to the adult table."

PFEIFFER: And what about Trump? What is he hoping to get out of this meeting?

SHIVARAM: I mean, I think part of this is drumming up a big photo op moment. Trump is coming to China after his own party didn't perform well in the midterm elections earlier this month. This is the first time he's on the world stage since then. And, you know, we've already seen and heard Trump start to talk about cementing his legacy as a president as he comes up in his last two years in the White House. So it's partly that.

PFEIFFER: And, Charles, it was Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, who proposed this gathering, is that right?

MAYNES: That's right. And, you know, throughout the war in Ukraine, you know, Putin has really sought to chip away at the West's attempts to isolate him over his actions in Ukraine. And so this is really a meeting - you know, an attempt to expand the meetings he's had with an array of world leaders whenever possible. But, you know, Sacha, it's hard to imagine a better one than this. You know, this is the company of the leaders of the U.S. and China, so optics matter here to Moscow, as well. This is proof Russia has reclaimed what it sees as its rightful place among global superpowers, even if economically Russia is by far the junior partner in this club.

Going in, there was a lot of talk here in Moscow about how this was a historic gathering where these three men would effectively decide the fate of the world. But Putin's primary objective is to steer conversations to the fate of Ukraine and impose a peace on Moscow's terms. You know, for Putin, that includes a new security framework for Europe that, if Russia got its way, would involve a major rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.

PFEIFFER: And Charles, Deepa mentioned the midterm election results in the U.S. as a factor in China. To what degree, if at all, does that apply to Russia, as well?

MAYNES: Well, Moscow is keenly aware that Democrats want to rein in Trump's outreach to Russia over the Ukraine issue, which means reining in deals and sanctions relief that Trump is offering the Kremlin in a bid to bring it to the negotiating table. So, you know, now it seems time for Russia to extract as much from that relationship with Trump as possible.

PFEIFFER: Jennifer, it's the president of China, Xi Jinping, who is the host. Is this a strategic, big power move on his part?

PAK: Oh, yeah. I mean, China is trying to show it can get major powers together. You know, China and the U.S., on the one hand, they're competing in all areas. It seems like every few weeks, there's another export control and then another threat to retaliate. But today, you know, Xi went to the airport to greet Trump. And for Russia, Xi and Putin had met today already. They reaffirmed their friendship, promoting this multipolar world. And in the past, together, they have denounced what they call unilateralism and hegemony - not so subtle digs at the U.S. And yet, Xi is now bringing all three of them together. This trilateral meeting really helps China project an image of itself as a predictable and stabilizing force.

PFEIFFER: Jennifer, headlines this week have included many stories about the NVIDIA spy scandal - the CEO of that company, Jensen Huang, forced to resign over revelations he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Has that come up in this meeting?

PAK: Not yet among the leaders, but they might do tomorrow when Trump and Xi meet before the trilateral meeting. On the surface, you see Trump and Xi very warm with each other. But structurally, the U.S.-China relationship remains very much the same. You know, this NVIDIA case has brought to the surface allegations of China trying to smuggle high-end U.S. chips, bypassing a U.S. ban, and of allegations of Chinese espionage.

Beijing, by the way, has denied the NVIDIA spy allegation, but this week, the Commerce Department has further restricted China's access to high-end chips. That could be a big hit to Chinese AI firms which are doing cutting-edge work. Whereas the Chinese Commerce Ministry and the Foreign Ministry - they've both condemned this, saying the U.S. is abusing export controls and overreaching with this concept of national security threats.

PFEIFFER: Deepa, there's a lot of tension in the Trump administration over China policy, and the Nvidia scandal has exacerbated that. How has that played out on this trip?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. It's interesting. I mean, as Jennifer was saying, the tensions between the U.S. and China have cooled down since last year's trade war. But there's still a lot of issues on the table - right? - when it comes to things like AI chips and, you know, things like are rare earths - exports on that. And that was highlighted in this recent NVIDIA scandal, to your point.

The tensions that you talk about that are playing out amid the Trump administration are also playing out here in China because two of Trump's Cabinet members are here in Shenzhen and are split on this issue - their approaches to China. That's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who's favoring a more lax policy towards China, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has a more hawkish approach. Trump has acknowledged that there's this split even among his own Cabinet members. And I'm curious, you know, how that divide plays out in these meetings here in Shenzhen but then, also, for after, when Trump goes back to Washington.

PFEIFFER: I'm interested in your views on whether anything concrete is expected to come from this meeting. Jennifer, your sense?

PAK: I mean, other than a photo of the three men, probably nothing substantial is expected. You know, as discussed, the potential topics - Trump wanting to talk about nuclear arms control. As Deepa mentioned, China has no interest. It has the smallest stockpile of nuclear weapons of the three. And previously, China's Foreign Ministry has said it is, quote, "unreasonable and unfeasible" to get China to talk about arms control at this stage. China really wants to guard what it has. On the topic of Ukraine, China has said this war is happening in Europe, so any negotiations should involve Europe.

PFEIFFER: And since there's not a European leader at this table, does that mean, Charles, very likely - unlikely for there to be a deal in Ukraine?

MAYNES: Well, it's certainly not looking great. China, while eager to support Russia economically, has preferred a more hands-off approach to Ukraine politically, as Jennifer is, you know, acknowledging here. Moreover, Putin's bilateral meeting with Trump sounds a bit in flux - Kremlin aids say it will happen, but it may be a fairly brief encounter. We'll have to see. But even if Putin, with support from Trump and Xi, wanted to impose a vision for peace on Ukraine and security for Europe, it's not at all clear they could. After all, the mere, you know, suggestion of Russia redefining European security has outraged the Europeans who ask, you know, why Russia is to be rewarded with this, particularly given Putin's actions in Ukraine.

You know, meanwhile, Kyiv has been flexing its muscles. Just this week, Ukrainian missiles destroyed a portion of a bridge that links the Russian mainland to Crimea. It's a symbol of Russia's hold over the peninsula it illegally seized back in 2014 and is widely considered a pet project of Vladimir Putin's. So, you know, clearly, Kyiv is not placing its hope it's on some peace imposed by Moscow. And this is something Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said repeatedly. Ukraine is fighting for the right to determine its own future.

PFEIFFER: That is Charles Maynes in Moscow, as well as Deepa Shivaram and Jennifer Pak in Shenzhen, China. Thanks to all three of you.

MAYNES: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: Democratic strategists think Montana House race could hold the secret to future wins
item.description: Montana last sent a Democrat to the U.S. House 32 years ago. That's the same year Montana's newest representative, Sam Forstag, was born. The former firefighter is now on Capitol Hill for freshman orientation, and his rise is giving Democrats a potential roadmap for competing in rural America. NPR's Kirk Siegler reports. KIRK SIEGLER, BYLINE: Montana has been solid Trump country since he was first
item.content:encoded:
Montana last sent a Democrat to the U.S. House 32 years ago. That's the same year Montana's newest representative, Sam Forstag, was born. The former firefighter is now on Capitol Hill for freshman orientation, and his rise is giving Democrats a potential roadmap for competing in rural America. NPR's Kirk Siegler reports.

KIRK SIEGLER, BYLINE: Montana has been solid Trump country since he was first elected president in 2016, and until the evening of November 3, it seemed like Democrats here could never figure out how to respond to his popularity.

SIEGLER: All that changed in dramatic fashion as Sam Forstag declared victory before a boisterous crowd of mostly young voters in the liberal college town of Missoula.

FORSTAG: We can again be a state that bends the course of this country's history for the better. The only way we fix this is we send working-class people to Washington so that we can go fight for ourselves.

SIEGLER: Montana hasn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. House for three decades. It's also been 10 years since any Democrat here won a statewide race. In the crowd, Whitney Williams sees his win as a sign that Democrats shouldn't write off rural America.

WHITNEY WILLIAMS: Democrats didn't do a good enough job with rural America, there's no question. But I think that that's changing, and I think it's changing pretty dramatically, and we can see it in these numbers tonight.

SIEGLER: How did he pull it off? Forstag didn't shy away from ripping on President Trump, casting him as a corrupt billionaire gutting public lands protections and public services. But he also blasted Democrats, saying he made barely 19 bucks an hour jumping out of airplanes into wildfires during the Biden administration. The day after the election, Forstag, in jeans and a Carhartt jacket, stood out in Missoula's freezing fog, holding what he said was his first-ever official press conference.

FORSTAG: Quite frankly, I don't care what party you're in. I just care that you're going to be out there working for working people.

SIEGLER: He said working people too many times to count.

In this huge district, from Glacier National Park to Yellowstone, people drive pickups to work and are fuming over high gas prices. And the national parks and federal lands agencies gutted by Trump's DOGE didn't sit well in tourism-dependent Montana either. Professor Lee Banville is a political analyst for Montana Public Radio.

LEE BANVILLE: He really has kind of laser-focused in on this message of, you know, it's not about turning Montana blue. It's about turning Montana blue collar.

SIEGLER: Banville thinks it's too early to tell whether Forstag will serve as a model for rural Democrats or if he just ran at the right time. The handsome former smokejumper was all over social media, looking rugged chic, working in the woods and blasting Trump for cutting hundreds of vital federal jobs here.

BANVILLE: In some ways, you know, kind of like Talarico, kind of like Ossoff, he's kind of made for TikTok. He's very quotable. He's running his campaign both as a broad effort but also as a real soundbite machine.

SIEGLER: Republican state legislator David Bedey says there just wasn't as much enthusiasm for Forstag's opponent, conservative radio host Aaron Flint. Bedey says Trump's policies like tariffs and the Iran war may have alienated some Montanans who voted for him in 2024.

DAVE BEDEY: I think it was largely the moment, but I'm going to give Forstag credit. He ran a great campaign. It's amazing how many people are fed up with both parties.

SIEGLER: Before Trump, Montana was famous for split-ticket voters. Whitney Williams says Forstag's win is a sign that's possible again. Her dad, the late Montana congressman Pat Williams, was the last Democrat to win this district.

WILLIAMS: Montanans like voting for people who are authentic and honest. And they're working people. And I think that we Democrats have fielded extraordinary candidates around this country.

SIEGLER: Now voters here say those candidates must actually deliver for working people, many of whom appear to have soured on the president and his MAGA movement.

Kirk Siegler, NPR News, Missoula, Montana.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.
